description:

title: Wire firmware.Load into the startup path so a mismatch refuses the boot
description:
TC-1.4 says 'refuses to START, naming the mismatch'. The loader refuses correctly and is proved at package level (TASK-1.7), but NOTHING CALLS IT: grep confirms firmware.Load appears only in its own tests, and neither cmd/goretrotv nor internal/app references the package. So half of TC-1.4 -- the half the test case actually names -- is unwired, and the phase would have closed with a loader nobody invokes.

Two gaps that are really one:
1. No startup path calls firmware.Load, so a checksum mismatch cannot refuse a boot that never consults it.
2. GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR does not exist in internal/config. p1-core correctly declined to add a config field nothing reads, and nothing reads it because nothing calls Load. Adding both together is what makes either coherent.

SCOPE:
- Add GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR to internal/config. Decide REQUIRED vs defaulted deliberately and state the reasoning: the test to apply is the one used for GORETROTV_ENV -- if a wrong guess means silently running a different ROM, it is required. The completeness test will force it into the committed example file.
- Call firmware.Load on the startup path so a mismatch, a missing image or a wrong size EXITS NON-ZERO naming the problem, before anything else initialises.
- This also closes the latent container trap: the image mounts firmware at /firmware while a relative firmware/ path works only because distroless sets no WORKDIR. Anything that later sets one turns this into a wrong-or-absent ROM, which is TC-1.4's own subject arriving through the back door.

PROOF (this is an instrument; watch it fail):
- Built binary, real firmware present -> starts.
- Built binary, one image corrupted -> exits non-zero naming the file and the digest mismatch.
- Built binary, firmware dir absent/empty -> exits non-zero naming what is missing.
- Assert the OUTCOME, not the absence of an exception: confirm the process did NOT reach 'listening'.

OWNERSHIP: p1-platform owns internal/config, internal/app and cmd/goretrotv. p1-core owns internal/firmware and must not edit those files. p1-core raised this rather than quietly widening scope into another agent's file, which is the correct call and why this is its own issue rather than a silent edit.

spec: plan/phase-1-foundation.md
close_reason:
Commit 6fdcc0d. Rewrote internal/config to load from the `env` struct tags by reflection rather than naming each variable a second time in hand-written code -- tags are now the single list, and Variables() is exported so Load and the completeness test read the same declaration and cannot drift. Added the example env file (committed; variable NAMES and harmless examples only, no secrets) and gitignored the operator's real copy, which was NOT ignored before.

GORETROTV_ENV is the required variable. Chosen because there is no safe guess between development and production: a box that quietly decided it was a development box is the failure that announces itself last. A test asserts no required variable has a default, since the default would be the guess the requirement exists to prevent.

TC-1.9 clause 1 (refuses the boot, naming the variable) PROVED END TO END against the built binary, not just in unit tests: with GORETROTV_ENV unset it exits 1 with `missing required environment variable: GORETROTV_ENV (see the example env file)`; with it set it starts, listens and shuts down gracefully. Unit tests also cover an empty/whitespace value counting as missing ("not exported" and "exported as nothing" look identical to an operator), all missing variables reported together rather than one per restart, and an unparseable value refused by name rather than silently left at its default.

TC-1.9 clause 2 (every variable appears in the example file, asserted by WALKING THE CONFIG STRUCT not by eye) implemented as a bidirectional reflect walk: a variable on the struct but not in the file is undocumented; a variable in the file but not on the struct is a line an operator would set and the binary would ignore, which is worse because it looks like it worked. The two ctl.sh-only variables are exempted by a short explicit allowlist in the test rather than by a section-heading heuristic, so widening the exemption is a deliberate edit. The walk uses platform/instrument.MustFind to assert it found its subject BEFORE asserting anything about it, so a walk that finds no fields cannot satisfy "every variable is documented" vacuously.

WATCHED IT FAIL, including the case the brief names explicitly: 6 mutants via go test -overlay, all 6 killed -- (1) an undocumented new field added to Config, killed with "GORETROTV_TRACE_DIR (Config.TraceDir) is read by the binary but is not in ../../.env.example"; (2) a stray variable left in the file with nothing reading it; (3) the walk finding nothing, killed by the subject assertion with "instrument examined nothing: found 0, expected at least 5"; (4) required no longer enforced; (5) a required variable given a default; (6) an unparseable value ignored. Zero survivors.

Also wired the requirement through the surfaces that would otherwise reintroduce the default: compose now uses the `:?` substitution rather than `:-` for GORETROTV_ENV (a compose-layer default would put the guess one level below the loader), and ctl.sh sources the operator's env file before running anything but deliberately does NOT create it, because a file conjured with defaults is precisely the silent default this task exists to refuse.

BONUS FIX, and it was a live instance of the decoration failure: ctl.sh's lint gate reported a pass while running twelve fewer linters than its name implies. golangci-lint installs to GOPATH/bin, which is not on PATH in a plain non-login shell, so `command -v golangci-lint` failed and the gate fell through to `warn "golangci-lint not on PATH; ran go vet only"` and exited 0. It now looks in GOPATH/bin and dies if it genuinely cannot find it.

go test -race clean on every package I own; golangci-lint 0 issues, exit code read directly rather than through a pipe. One justified nolint on the reflect.Kind switch (exhaustive false positive -- the default case returns an error rather than skipping, which is the thing that linter exists to catch).

NOTE FOR THE LEAD: ./ctl.sh run and ./ctl.sh up now require the operator to create their env file from the example (one cp). That is the deliverable working as specified, not a regression, and ctl.sh warns with the exact command. Flagged to the team.

title: [TASK-1.4] GitHub Actions: vet, staticcheck, `go test -race`, build
description:
GitHub Actions: vet, staticcheck, `go test -race`, build

-> /go-engineer
[no-test: CI config proven by a deliberately failing run]
spec: plan/phase-1-foundation.md
close_reason:
Commit b23052b, .github/workflows/ci.yml. Ten steps: checkout, setup-go (1.22, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, cache off), report the toolchain, assert the module graph still holds exactly one module, gofmt, go vet ./..., golangci-lint (staticcheck runs inside it -- .golangci.yml is v2 format and enables it there, so a separate step would be a second copy of the same config), go test -race ./..., and build. Triggers on push to master, every pull request, and workflow_dispatch, with concurrency cancel-in-progress.

THE PARENTHETICAL WAS A REQUIREMENT AND I MET IT -- GitHub was reachable from here and gh was authenticated, so this was proved against the real service rather than reasoned about:

- Run 35125387014 went RED. A scratch branch (ci-proof) carried the workflow plus a deliberately failing test; CI failed on exactly the `go test -race` step, and the log names the assertion: "--- FAIL: TestDeliberateFailureToProveCIGoesRed ... this test fails on purpose; if CI is green with this present, CI is not running the tests". Every other step passed, so the red was the test step and nothing else.
- Run 35125645626 went GREEN, all ten steps, after removing only that test. The workflow file on that run was verified byte-identical (diff -q) to the file committed here.

I used a deliberately FAILING TEST rather than a vet error or unformatted code on purpose: those are caught by our own pre-commit hook from TASK-1.3, and bypassing one guard with --no-verify to test another would have been the wrong trade.

HYGIENE: the proof ran in a `git worktree`, so the shared working tree was never checked out from under p1-core. origin/master was never touched and is still at f54e9bf. The throwaway pull request (#1, opened draft, titled DO NOT MERGE) is closed with an explanatory comment, the ci-proof branch is deleted from origin and locally, and the worktree is removed. Verified afterwards by `git ls-remote`.

THE RED RUN ALSO CAUGHT A REAL STALENESS PROBLEM, which is the value of actually running it: actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-go@v5 and golangci-lint-action@v8 all still declare the node20 runtime, which GitHub removed from the runners today (2026-09-16) and is now force-migrating to node24. I verified the current majors against each action's own action.yml through the GitHub API rather than trusting a search summary or guessing a tag -- a wrong tag would have made CI red for everyone -- and moved to checkout@v7, setup-go@v7 and golangci-lint-action@v9. Confirmed from the v9 README that it is v8 plus the node24 runtime and keeps v8's `golangci-lint >= v2.1.0` constraint, so the linter stays pinned at v2.1.6, the exact version installed locally. CI and a developer machine therefore run identical linters; a gate that finds different things in the two places is one people learn to ignore. The green run carries no annotations.

BEYOND THE NAMED FOUR, one added step: the module graph is asserted to hold exactly one module. ADR 0001 records the no-dependency rule as a floor rather than a vow, and a later phase that genuinely needs a dependency should take one -- what it rules out is acquiring dependencies by default, before a requirement names them, which happens when somebody runs `go get` and nobody notices. Taking one deliberately now means editing that step, which is the point. Phase 1a may want to own this as a formal conformance rule instead; it is a two-line move if so.

Also ran the workflow's exact command sequence locally against the current tree before touching CI: all six checks green, including p1-core's internal/bus, internal/memory and internal/firmware.

NOT INCLUDED, deliberately: govulncheck. ADR 0001 records that it still matters because stdlib vulnerabilities are now the only category we can have, but installing it needs a version that builds under Go 1.22 and I was not willing to ship a step whose install I had guessed at. ./ctl.sh vuln covers it locally. Worth a follow-up issue once someone pins a 1.22-compatible version.

title: [TASK-1.3] `.githooks/pre-commit` (credential guard + bd mirror check) and `core.hooksPath`; `.claude
description:
`.githooks/pre-commit` (credential guard + bd mirror check) and `core.hooksPath`; `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json` so the loop travels with the repo

-> /go-engineer
[no-test: hook verified by running it directly]
spec: plan/phase-1-foundation.md
close_reason:
Commit 9f76a27, and core.hooksPath is now ARMED at .githooks in this working copy.

Shipped: .githooks/pre-commit (framework credential guard, copied not symlinked so the repo works on a machine without the framework, plus an appended Go hygiene block), four delegator hooks (pre-push, post-merge, post-checkout, prepare-commit-msg), a merged .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json.

THE BEADS COLLISION, resolved without losing anything: bd init had set core.hooksPath to .beads/hooks. Pointing it at .githooks naively would have silently disabled all five beads hooks -- no error, just a tracker that quietly stops exporting. Each .githooks hook now runs its .beads counterpart afterwards; the four that have no project-specific work exist solely to keep that delegation alive. The beads hooks are tracked in git, so this survives a fresh clone.

Go hygiene is scoped deliberately. gofmt runs against STAGED content, not the working tree, because several agents work this tree at once and the two are routinely different -- a hook judging the working tree would pass or fail on somebody else's half-finished edit. go vet needs a whole package to compile so it cannot see staged content alone; it runs over the packages the staged files belong to rather than ./... so a teammate mid-edit in an unrelated package cannot block a commit nobody can fix. A guard that fails for reasons you cannot act on is one people learn to bypass.

settings.json was MERGED, not overwritten: the existing bd SessionStart hook is intact. Permissions allow the read-only and check verbs (status/logs/health/build/test/lint/fmt/vuln) and leave the shared-state ones (up/down/restart/run/clean) to ask. Deny covers the secret-bearing paths, with the example env file explicitly allowed so the config completeness test can read it.

PROVED THE HOOK CAN FAIL, in a `git clone` to a temp dir so the shared index was never touched, and having first confirmed the hook that would run resolved to a path INSIDE the clone: (1) a fake GitHub token in an added line -> REFUSED, naming the file and line; (2) an unformatted staged Go file -> REFUSED, naming the file and the fix; (3) a go vet error in a package being committed -> REFUSED, quoting vet's message; (4) a shell script that does not parse -> REFUSED; (5) the control, a clean formatted Go file -> ACCEPTED, and its output carries beads' own message, which is the evidence the delegation actually runs. Then armed it in the real repo and ran the armed hook against the live index: exit 0.

FINDING WORTH RECORDING, and it cost me the first run of this proof: my cleanup step used `git clean -fd`, which deleted the then-untracked .githooks directory, and GIT SILENTLY RUNS NO HOOKS AT ALL when core.hooksPath points at a directory that does not exist -- no warning, no non-zero exit, every commit sails through ungated and green. Four of my five proof cases reported false passes before I caught it. The proof harness now asserts the hook is still present before trusting any result, which is the same discipline as asserting an instrument found its subject before asserting what it found. Committing the hooks is what makes this safe in the real repo, but the failure mode is worth knowing about: an absent .githooks on some branch or worktree means an unguarded commit that looks exactly like a guarded one.

NOT PROVED, and I am saying so rather than implying otherwise: the guard's secret-bearing-FILENAME branch (case 3 of the framework template). This session's own safety policy blocks any shell command naming a path that looks like key material or a credentials store, which is precisely what that fixture requires. The branch is verbatim framework code that I did not modify, and the two branches I did modify are both proven above. To close it by hand, in a throwaway clone: create a file named like key material, `git add -f` it, and commit -- expect "refusing to commit a key material: <path>".

One operational note: core.hooksPath is local repo config and is not carried by a clone. CLAUDE.md -> Conventions already documents the command. If beads re-runs its installer it may point hooksPath back at .beads/hooks, which would drop the credential guard silently; worth a check if hooks ever seem not to fire.

title: [TASK-1.2] Structured JSON logging carrying `icount` alongside wall time, because every question here
description:

spec: plan/phase-1-foundation.md
close_reason: Extended internal/logging in place (no second package) with icount.go: Counter (one method, Now() uint64 -- *clock.Clock satisfies it), WithCounter(logger, counter), and ICountKey. Commit df7d73a. TC-1.1 PROVED: a single log line carries both icount and an RFC3339 wall timestamp, and the icount matches the machine -- the test drives a REAL clock.Clock advanced 4,500,000 instructions rather than a stub, so it also proves the two packages agree on what now means. The count is read at emit time, not at logger construction: a logger built at instruction 0 and held across three Advances logs 1000/3000/6000. Absent-vs-zero rule enforced: a logger with no machine behind it emits NO icount field, because icount=0 is a real instruction and indistinguishable from the start of a boot. The handler owns grouping rather than delegating it, so icount stays at the top level under WithGroup and nested groups -- buried in a group it is readable by a human and invisible to the query that is the field's only purpose. WATCHED IT FAIL: 4 mutants via go test -overlay, all killed -- frozen/stale icount, icount buried in the group, nil counter logging a plausible zero, Enabled no longer delegating level filtering. go test -race clean; golangci-lint 0 issues (fixed 2 real findings, prealloc and a redundant staticcheck QF1011 type assertion, rather than suppressing). NOTE for the lead: WithCounter is not yet wired into a running machine because no machine exists yet -- cmd/goretrotv builds only the HTTP server. Wiring is one line (logging.WithCounter(logger, machine)) at the point the instruction loop is constructed, and belongs with whoever builds it.

title: Add govulncheck to CI, pinned to a version that builds under Go 1.22
description:
Deliberately left out of TASK-1.4. ADR 0001 records that govulncheck still matters precisely BECAUSE the dependency set is empty: standard-library CVEs are now the only category this project can have, so the vulnerability surface is entirely stdlib and entirely invisible without this step.

It was omitted rather than guessed because installing it needs a version that builds under Go 1.22 (the host ceiling -- no fetchable newer toolchain), and shipping a CI step whose install command was guessed at is how a gate arrives broken or, worse, silently skipped. That was the right call.
